questions.passage: Common sense suggests that the more options we have, the happier we will be. A shopper faced with forty varieties of jam ought, in theory, to be better served than one offered only six. Yet a body of research beginning in the late 1990s challenged this assumption. In one widely discussed experiment, a stall displaying a large selection of products attracted more visitors but generated far fewer sales than a stall with a small selection. The proposed explanation was that abundant choice can be paralysing: when the alternatives are numerous and similar, deciding becomes effortful, and the fear of choosing badly leads people to avoid choosing at all. Even those who do decide may end up less satisfied, haunted by the thought that a better option was left on the shelf. Later attempts to replicate these findings, however, produced mixed results, and a large review concluded that the average effect of extra choice was close to zero. The consensus now is more nuanced. Too much choice appears to be a problem mainly when people lack clear preferences, when the options are hard to compare, or when they are under time pressure.

questions.passage: Machine translation has improved so rapidly in recent years that some observers have predicted the end of the translation profession. Professional translators tend to respond with a weary smile. Software, they point out, is now extremely good at producing fluent sentences, and for routine documents such as product manuals it can save enormous amounts of time. Fluency, however, is not the same as accuracy. A machine may render a legal clause in perfectly smooth prose while quietly reversing its meaning, and because the output reads so naturally, such errors are harder to spot than the clumsy mistakes of older systems. Literary texts pose a different difficulty. A novelist's choice of a slightly unusual word, or a pun that works only in the original language, demands an interpretive decision that no statistical model can make on the author's behalf. What has changed is the nature of the work. Many translators now spend less time translating from scratch and more time checking and refining machine output, a task some find tedious and others regard as a welcome way of handling larger volumes. Few expect the human role to vanish; most expect it to keep shifting.

This so-called urban heat island effect is caused largely by materials such as asphalt and concrete, which absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night. Trees counter the effect in two ways: their canopies shade the ground, and they release water vapour through their leaves, which cools the surrounding air. As heatwaves become more frequent, many city authorities have announced ambitious tree-planting targets. Planting, however, is the easy part. A young tree in a narrow pavement pit, surrounded by compacted soil and exposed to pollution, may struggle to survive its first few years, and in some programmes a significant proportion of new trees have died before reaching maturity. Experts therefore argue that targets should be measured not by the number of saplings put in the ground but by the area of canopy that is still growing a decade later. That shift would require long-term budgets for watering and maintenance, which are far less photogenic than a mayor holding a spade.

questions.passage: Few debates in the museum world are as charged as the one over restitution: the return of objects acquired during periods of colonial rule to the countries from which they were taken. For decades, many major institutions argued that they were the best guardians of such treasures, able to conserve them expertly and to display them to millions of visitors from around the world. Critics replied that this reasoning conveniently ignored how the objects had been obtained, often through looting, coercion or deeply unequal deals. In recent years the balance of opinion has shifted noticeably. Several museums have returned items, sometimes after years of negotiation, and some governments have changed laws that previously prevented national collections from giving anything away. The process is rarely straightforward. Establishing exactly how an object left its place of origin can require painstaking research, and disputes can arise over who the rightful recipient is when borders and communities have changed. Nevertheless, a growing number of curators now see restitution less as a loss than as an opportunity to build lasting partnerships with the places where their collections began.

questions.passage: Buried within the ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland lies one of the most detailed records of the planet's past climate. Each year, snow falls on the surface and is gradually compressed into ice by the weight of later snowfall, trapping tiny bubbles of air as it does so. By drilling deep cores and analysing these bubbles, scientists can measure the composition of the atmosphere as it was hundreds of thousands of years ago. The chemistry of the ice itself reveals past temperatures, while layers of ash record volcanic eruptions that occurred long before any written history. The picture that emerges is striking. Over the period covered by the oldest cores, levels of carbon dioxide rose and fell in step with the cycle of ice ages, but they never approached the levels measured in the air today. The work is slow and costly; a single deep core can take several seasons to extract in some of the harshest conditions on Earth. Researchers are now searching for sites containing ice more than a million years old, hoping to understand a puzzling change in the rhythm of the ice ages that took place around that time.

questions.passage: Astronomers have long been troubled by a discrepancy that refuses to go away. When they measure how fast stars orbit the centres of their galaxies, the outer stars turn out to be moving far too quickly; given the visible matter alone, they ought to be flung off into intergalactic space. The most widely accepted explanation is that galaxies are embedded in vast halos of so-called dark matter, a substance that neither emits nor absorbs light and reveals itself only through its gravitational pull. Yet decades of increasingly sensitive experiments, many conducted deep underground to shield detectors from cosmic rays, have failed to catch a single particle of it. A minority of physicists contend that this silence is telling. Rather than postulating an invisible ingredient, they propose that our understanding of gravity itself breaks down at very low accelerations. Their modified theories account remarkably well for the rotation of individual galaxies, but they struggle to explain the behaviour of galaxy clusters and the pattern of radiation left over from the early universe, where dark matter models perform far better. For the time being, neither camp can claim outright victory, and the question remains one of the most consequential open problems in physics.

questions.passage: Few creatures have acquired a reputation as outsized as that of the tardigrade, a plump, eight-legged animal rarely longer than a millimetre. Popular accounts describe it as virtually indestructible, and the claims are not wholly unfounded. When its surroundings dry out, a tardigrade can expel almost all of its body water, curl into a shrivelled state known as a tun, and suspend its metabolism to the point where it is barely distinguishable from a dead organism. In this condition, specimens have withstood extreme cold, intense radiation and even exposure to the vacuum of space, reviving within hours once rehydrated. Researchers have identified a family of proteins unique to these animals that seem to form a glass-like matrix inside cells, protecting delicate structures from damage as water disappears. It would be a mistake, however, to regard tardigrades as invulnerable. In their active, hydrated state they are surprisingly fragile, and several studies suggest that prolonged warming of their habitats could harm them more than any laboratory ordeal. Their resilience, in other words, is a strategy for enduring brief catastrophes, not a licence to thrive in permanently hostile conditions.

questions.passage: When a new drug is tested, patients in a control group are routinely given an inert tablet so that researchers can separate the genuine effects of the medicine from the improvement people experience simply because they expect to get better. This placebo response has traditionally been treated as a nuisance, a statistical noise to be subtracted. Over the past two decades, however, it has become an object of study in its own right. Brain-imaging experiments have shown that expectation can trigger the release of the body's own pain-relieving chemicals, which suggests that the effect is far from imaginary. More startling still are trials of so-called open-label placebos, in which patients are told plainly that their pills contain no active ingredient. Remarkably, some of these patients, particularly those with chronic pain or irritable bowel conditions, report meaningful relief. Sceptics caution that subjective symptoms are notoriously malleable and that patients may be reporting what they think the doctor wants to hear. Nonetheless, the findings have prompted a rethink of the ritual surrounding treatment, from the warmth of the consultation to the colour of the capsule, as factors that may themselves contribute to healing.

questions.passage: It is sometimes said that the age of antibiotics will be remembered as a brief golden interlude between two eras of untreatable infection. The remark is deliberately provocative, but the underlying concern is shared by most public-health authorities. Every time an antibiotic is used, bacteria that happen to carry resistance genes gain an advantage over their susceptible neighbours, and because bacteria can swap genetic material with one another, resistance can spread across species with alarming speed. Overprescription in human medicine bears part of the blame, yet in many countries the bulk of antibiotics is administered to livestock, often to promote growth rather than to treat disease. Compounding the problem is a stark economic reality: a new antibiotic that works well will, quite rightly, be held in reserve and used as sparingly as possible, which means it is unlikely ever to earn back the cost of its development. Several large pharmaceutical companies have consequently abandoned the field. Proposed remedies include public funding for research, guaranteed payments to developers regardless of sales volume, and stricter controls on agricultural use, though none of these has yet been adopted on anything like the scale experts consider necessary.

questions.passage: For much of the twentieth century, the bacteria living in the human gut were regarded, if they were considered at all, as passive lodgers. That view has been comprehensively overturned. The trillions of microbes inhabiting our intestines are now known to help digest fibre, synthesise certain vitamins and train the immune system to distinguish friend from foe. More controversially, a growing body of research links the composition of this microbial community to conditions as varied as obesity, depression and autoimmune disease. Such findings have fuelled a booming market in probiotic supplements and home testing kits, many of which promise to rebalance the gut and transform the customer's health. Researchers tend to be considerably more guarded than the marketing. Much of the evidence comes from studies in mice raised in sterile conditions, whose biology differs from ours in important respects, and in human studies it is often unclear whether a particular microbial profile causes a disease or merely accompanies it. Moreover, the gut ecosystem varies so much between individuals that a supplement beneficial to one person may do nothing for another. The science is genuinely exciting, but its practical applications, most experts agree, remain largely in their infancy.

questions.passage: Anyone who has crammed for an examination late into the night may be dismayed to learn how strongly the evidence favours the opposite approach. Sleep, it turns out, is not merely a period of rest during which the brain idles; it is an active phase in which recently acquired information is sorted, strengthened and integrated with what we already know. During deep sleep, the hippocampus, a structure crucial for forming new memories, appears to replay the day's experiences, transferring them gradually to the cortex for longer-term storage. Dreaming sleep, by contrast, seems to play a part in extracting general patterns and in softening the emotional charge of distressing events. Experiments in which volunteers learn a task and are then either allowed to sleep or kept awake consistently show that the sleepers perform better when tested later, sometimes even arriving at insights that eluded them before. None of this means that a single good night can compensate for weeks of neglect, nor that people can learn new material simply by listening to recordings as they doze; such claims have little support. What the research does suggest is that sacrificing sleep in order to study longer is, more often than not, a false economy.

questions.passage: Coral reefs occupy a tiny fraction of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. Their brilliance depends on a delicate partnership: the coral animal houses microscopic algae within its tissues, and the algae, in return, supply most of the energy the coral needs through photosynthesis. When the surrounding water becomes unusually warm, this arrangement breaks down. Stressed corals expel their algae and turn a ghostly white, a process known as bleaching. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead; if temperatures fall quickly enough, the algae can return and the colony may recover. Repeated or prolonged heatwaves, however, leave corals starved and vulnerable to disease, and large stretches of reef have died in recent decades. Some scientists are experimenting with breeding heat-tolerant corals or transplanting fragments onto damaged sites, and such projects have produced encouraging local results. Critics point out that the scale of these interventions is minuscule compared with the scale of the damage, and warn that they risk distracting attention from the only lasting solution, which is to curb the emissions that are warming the oceans in the first place.

questions.passage: The term rewilding covers a surprisingly broad spectrum of ideas. At one end lie modest projects that remove drainage ditches from a patch of farmland and let it revert to scrub; at the other, ambitious schemes that reintroduce large herbivores and even predators to landscapes from which they vanished centuries ago. What unites them is a willingness to step back and allow natural processes, rather than human management, to shape the land. Advocates point to striking successes: the return of beavers, for instance, has in some places created wetlands that slow floods, filter water and teem with insects and birds. Yet the approach is far from universally welcomed. Farmers fear for their livestock and their livelihoods, rural communities sometimes perceive the projects as an imposition by distant urban elites, and some conservationists argue that certain cherished habitats, such as flower-rich meadows, exist only because of centuries of grazing and mowing and would be lost if left alone. The most durable projects, observers note, tend to be those that involve local people from the outset and offer them tangible benefits, whether through tourism, compensation schemes or simply a voice in the decisions being made.

questions.passage: Among the technologies proposed to limit climate change, few provoke such divided reactions as carbon capture. The principle is straightforward: carbon dioxide is separated from the exhaust of power stations or factories, compressed and pumped into deep geological formations, where it can in theory remain for thousands of years. A more recent variant, direct air capture, extracts the gas from the atmosphere itself. Supporters insist that some form of carbon removal is indispensable, because certain industries, such as cement production, emit carbon dioxide as an unavoidable by-product of their chemistry. Opponents do not necessarily dispute this, but they object to the way the technology is often presented. Capture plants are expensive and energy-hungry, and the quantities removed so far are a negligible fraction of global emissions. More worryingly, they argue, the promise of future capture can serve as a convenient justification for continuing to burn fossil fuels today, on the assumption that the damage can be undone later. Many analysts take an intermediate position: carbon capture has a legitimate but narrow role, best reserved for emissions that genuinely cannot be eliminated by other means.

Citizen science, as it is known, nonetheless raises legitimate questions about reliability. Untrained observers may misidentify species, and volunteers tend to cluster in wealthy, accessible areas, leaving remote regions underrepresented. Project designers have developed ingenious ways of addressing these concerns, from requiring several independent classifications of each image to using statistical techniques that correct for uneven sampling. Advocates also stress benefits that go beyond the data themselves: participants frequently report a deeper understanding of scientific methods and a stronger attachment to the natural world, outcomes that may prove as significant, in the long run, as any individual discovery.

questions.passage: Peer review, the process by which scientific papers are scrutinised by independent experts before publication, is often described as the gold standard of research quality. Those who know it best tend to describe it in more equivocal terms. Reviewers are usually unpaid, overburdened and anonymous, and they typically have neither the time nor the access to raw data required to detect fraud or subtle errors. Experiments in which deliberate mistakes were inserted into manuscripts found that many reviewers failed to notice most of them. The system can also be conservative, favouring work that confirms established ideas and treating genuinely original approaches with suspicion. At the same time, it would be rash to dismiss peer review altogether. It frequently improves the clarity of papers, catches obvious flaws and obliges authors to justify their claims more carefully. Reformers have proposed a range of alternatives, including publishing reviewers' reports alongside articles, posting papers publicly before review so that a wider community can comment, and continuing to evaluate studies after publication. What is increasingly recognised is that peer review is a filter rather than a guarantee, and that the publication of a finding is the beginning of its scrutiny, not the end.

questions.passage: Only a few decades ago, nobody knew for certain whether any star other than the sun possessed planets. Thousands have since been detected, most of them indirectly, by observing the slight dimming of a star as a planet passes in front of it. That same technique now allows astronomers to do something that once seemed fanciful: to analyse the atmospheres of these distant worlds. As starlight filters through a planet's atmosphere during a transit, certain wavelengths are absorbed by particular gases, leaving a characteristic signature that powerful telescopes can decode. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane have all been identified in this way. The ultimate ambition is to detect so-called biosignatures, combinations of gases that, on Earth at least, are produced chiefly by living organisms. Researchers are acutely aware of the dangers of premature announcements. Several gases once proposed as signs of life can also be generated by volcanic activity, chemical reactions or even quirks in the data, and a number of tantalising detections have later been called into question. Any claim to have found life beyond Earth, astronomers agree, will require multiple independent lines of evidence and a great deal of patience.

questions.passage: Each autumn, countless birds set off on journeys of thousands of kilometres, often travelling at night and over open sea, and many return the following spring to the very same patch of woodland. How they navigate with such precision remains one of the most intriguing questions in biology. It is now well established that birds draw on several cues, including the position of the sun, the patterns of the stars and, in some species, familiar landmarks and smells. The most mysterious of their senses, however, is their apparent ability to perceive the Earth's magnetic field. One leading hypothesis proposes that a light-sensitive protein in the bird's eye undergoes a quantum chemical reaction influenced by magnetism, possibly allowing the bird to see the field as a pattern superimposed on its vision. Another suggests that tiny particles of magnetic iron, perhaps located in the beak or the inner ear, act as a kind of compass. Evidence exists for both mechanisms, and they may well operate side by side. Experiments showing that weak radio interference from electrical equipment can disrupt birds' orientation have added an unexpected urban dimension to the research.

questions.passage: Beneath the floor of almost every forest lies an intricate web of fungal threads that intertwine with the roots of trees. This partnership is ancient and well documented: the fungi help trees absorb water and nutrients from the soil, and in exchange receive sugars that the trees produce through photosynthesis. In recent decades, a more romantic picture has gained enormous popularity. According to this view, the fungal networks link entire forests into a kind of underground internet through which mature trees nourish their offspring, warn neighbours of insect attacks and even share resources with ailing members of the community. Books and documentaries have presented this cooperative vision as established fact. A number of forest ecologists have recently voiced misgivings. Reviewing the field studies, they argue that the evidence that resources travel between trees through fungal links in meaningful quantities is surprisingly thin, and that alternative explanations, such as transfer through the soil, have not always been ruled out. They do not deny that fungal partnerships are vital to forest health; their objection is to the leap from intriguing but limited findings to sweeping claims that have captured the public imagination far faster than the data warrant.

questions.passage: Across vast stretches of the far north, the ground has remained frozen for thousands of years. This permafrost holds an immense store of carbon in the form of plant and animal remains that never decomposed because the cold preserved them, by some estimates roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere currently contains. As the Arctic warms faster than almost anywhere else on the planet, this frozen ground is beginning to thaw. Microbes that had been dormant awaken and start to break down the organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane, a gas that traps heat far more effectively over the short term. Scientists fear a feedback loop in which warming releases greenhouse gases that cause further warming. The physical consequences are already visible locally: roads buckle, buildings tilt as their foundations subside, and in some places the ground collapses abruptly, forming new lakes and craters. Estimating the global impact is difficult, because the speed of thaw varies enormously from place to place and because newly exposed soils may also support plants that absorb some carbon. Most projections nonetheless indicate that permafrost will become a significant additional source of emissions over the coming century.

questions.passage: With freshwater supplies under growing pressure from population growth and drought, an increasing number of countries are turning to the one source that seems inexhaustible: the sea. Desalination, the removal of salt from seawater, is now practised on a large scale, particularly in arid regions of the Middle East, and its costs have fallen markedly thanks to advances in reverse osmosis, which forces water through membranes fine enough to hold back salt. Yet the technology is no panacea. Desalination plants consume considerable amounts of energy, which, if supplied by fossil fuels, adds to the greenhouse emissions that are worsening droughts in the first place. They also produce brine, a highly concentrated salty residue, which is usually discharged back into the sea, where it can sink and harm creatures living on the seabed. Engineers are exploring ways to dilute the brine more effectively or to extract valuable minerals from it, and plants powered by renewable energy are increasingly common. Water specialists nevertheless caution that desalination should complement rather than replace less glamorous measures, such as repairing leaking pipes, recycling wastewater and using water more efficiently in agriculture.

questions.passage: Stacked trays of lettuce glowing under pink lights in a disused warehouse have become a favourite image of the future of food. Vertical farms grow crops indoors, usually without soil, with every variable, from temperature to the composition of the nutrient solution, precisely controlled. The advantages are considerable: yields per square metre far exceed those of open fields, pesticides are largely unnecessary, water is recycled, and produce can be grown close to the cities where it is consumed, regardless of climate or season. Investors poured money into the sector, and some companies promised to transform agriculture. Several of those companies have since collapsed. The fundamental obstacle is energy. The sun provides light to conventional farms free of charge, whereas indoor farms must replace it with electricity, along with heating, cooling and ventilation. When energy prices rose sharply, many operations found their costs impossible to sustain. The economics work best for small, fast-growing, high-value crops such as herbs and salad leaves; staple crops such as wheat or rice, which supply most of the world's calories, remain far too cheap to grow outdoors for indoor cultivation to compete.

questions.passage: Discussions of the ethics of self-driving cars have often revolved around dramatic dilemmas. Should a vehicle whose brakes have failed swerve to avoid a group of pedestrians if doing so means killing its own passenger? Large online surveys asking millions of people to resolve such scenarios have revealed intriguing cultural differences in moral preferences. Many engineers, however, regard the obsession with these thought experiments as a distraction. Real collisions rarely present clear-cut choices between known victims, and a car's software is far more likely to fail through misjudging an unusual situation, such as a cyclist behaving unpredictably or a road sign obscured by snow, than through confronting a philosophical puzzle. The more pressing ethical questions, they argue, are mundane but consequential: how safe must autonomous vehicles be before they are permitted on public roads, who bears legal responsibility when one causes harm, and how should companies report the incidents that occur during testing? There is also the matter of comparison. Human drivers cause an enormous number of deaths each year, so a technology that is imperfect but substantially safer could save many lives, even though each accident it causes will attract disproportionate attention.

questions.passage: Modern messaging applications commonly use end-to-end encryption, a method that scrambles messages so that only the sender and recipient can read them; not even the company operating the service holds the keys. Law-enforcement agencies have long complained that this leaves them unable to access the communications of criminals and terrorists, even with a court order, and some governments have pressed technology firms to build in a mechanism, often dubbed a backdoor, that would allow authorised officials to read messages when necessary. Security experts are almost unanimous in opposing the idea. Their objection is not primarily political but technical: there is no known way to create an access point that only the good guys can use. Any deliberate weakness, they argue, would sooner or later be discovered and exploited by hostile states or criminal hackers, endangering the private data of millions of ordinary users, including businesses, journalists and dissidents. Officials retort that the companies are capable of extraordinary innovation and could find a solution if they wished. The impasse has persisted for years, with policymakers alternately advancing and withdrawing proposals while the underlying mathematical dilemma remains unresolved.

Components are glued rather than screwed together, spare parts and diagrams are available only to authorised technicians, and some devices refuse to function with replacement parts unless these are activated by the manufacturer's software. Manufacturers defend such practices on grounds of safety, quality and the protection of their intellectual property, arguing that amateur repairs can damage products or even cause injury. Critics see a more cynical motive: discouraging repair pushes consumers towards buying new products, a cycle that generates vast quantities of electronic waste, one of the fastest-growing waste streams in the world. The right-to-repair movement, which brings together environmental campaigners, independent repair shops and farmers frustrated at being unable to fix their own tractors, has scored notable successes. Several jurisdictions have passed laws obliging manufacturers to make spare parts and repair information available for a set number of years. Some companies, having resisted such measures, now sell repair kits directly to customers, although campaigners complain that the kits are sometimes so cumbersome as to deter all but the most determined.

questions.passage: Loneliness has traditionally been regarded as a private sorrow rather than a matter for doctors. A substantial body of research now challenges that view. Large studies following people over many years have found that those who report persistent loneliness or social isolation face a markedly higher risk of heart disease, stroke, dementia and early death, with some researchers comparing the effect to that of well-known hazards such as smoking. The mechanisms are not yet fully understood, but chronic loneliness appears to keep the body in a state of heightened alert, raising levels of stress hormones and inflammation and disrupting sleep. It may also make people less likely to exercise, eat well or seek medical help. Importantly, loneliness is not the same as being alone: some people live solitary lives contentedly, while others feel isolated amid a crowded household. In response, a number of governments have appointed ministers or launched strategies to tackle the problem, and some health services now practise so-called social prescribing, referring patients to community groups, volunteering or arts activities rather than, or in addition to, prescribing medicine. Evaluations of such schemes are still at an early stage, and the evidence of their effectiveness is mixed.

questions.passage: Some years ago, a study of judges deciding whether to grant parole appeared to reveal something alarming: the likelihood of a favourable ruling was highest at the start of the day and immediately after meal breaks, and declined steadily as each session wore on. The finding was widely cited as evidence of decision fatigue, the idea that making choices depletes a limited mental resource, so that people faced with a long series of decisions increasingly fall back on the easiest option, which for a judge is usually to refuse. The theory had intuitive appeal and spawned advice ranging from scheduling important meetings in the morning to wearing the same clothes every day. Subsequent scrutiny has been less kind. Critics pointed out that the order in which cases were heard was not random; prisoners without legal representation, whose applications were weaker, tended to be scheduled at the end of sessions. Meanwhile, the laboratory experiments underpinning the broader theory of depleted willpower have largely failed to replicate. Mental fatigue is undoubtedly real, but the claim that it systematically distorts expert judgement in this particular way now looks considerably shakier than it once did.

questions.passage: Most people have experienced moments in which they become so absorbed in an activity that time seems to vanish, self-consciousness falls away and effort feels almost effortless. A psychologist who interviewed artists, athletes, surgeons and chess players about such experiences coined the term flow to describe them. His research identified several conditions under which flow is most likely to arise. The activity must have clear goals and provide immediate feedback, so that the person knows at every moment how well they are doing. Above all, there must be a balance between challenge and skill: a task that is too easy produces boredom, while one that is too hard generates anxiety. Flow emerges in the narrow channel between the two, which is why it tends to require continual adjustment as skills improve. Intriguingly, his surveys suggested that people often experienced flow more frequently at work than during leisure, even though they claimed to prefer leisure, since passive pastimes such as watching television rarely offer the necessary challenge. The concept has since been applied to education, sport and the design of video games, though critics note that the same absorption can also make certain activities, including gambling, dangerously compelling.

questions.passage: Over the past half-century, allergies, asthma and certain autoimmune diseases have become dramatically more common in wealthy countries. In the late 1980s, a researcher noticed that children from large families, who were presumably exposed to more infections from their siblings, were less likely to develop hay fever. From this observation grew the hygiene hypothesis: the notion that modern cleanliness deprives the developing immune system of the microbial encounters it needs in order to calibrate itself, leaving it prone to overreact to harmless substances. The idea has been substantially revised since then. Researchers now emphasise not infections as such, which carry serious risks of their own, but regular exposure to the diverse, largely harmless microbes found in soil, animals and natural environments, with which humans evolved. Children raised on traditional farms, for instance, show strikingly low rates of allergy. Experts are keen to dispel a popular misreading of the hypothesis. It offers no justification for abandoning hand-washing or household cleaning, which prevent the spread of dangerous pathogens. Spending time outdoors, contact with animals and a varied diet are considered far more relevant than any reluctance to clean the kitchen.

questions.passage: A century ago, before the discovery of penicillin, a number of doctors experimented with an unusual treatment for bacterial infections: viruses known as bacteriophages, or phages, which infect and destroy bacteria while leaving human cells untouched. Phages are astonishingly abundant, inhabiting virtually every environment in which bacteria live, and each type typically attacks only a narrow range of bacterial strains. When antibiotics arrived, offering broad and reliable protection, phage therapy was largely abandoned in the West, although research continued in parts of Eastern Europe. The spread of antibiotic resistance has revived interest. In a handful of widely reported cases, patients with infections that had defeated every available drug recovered after receiving phages carefully matched to their particular bacteria. Turning such successes into routine medicine is far from straightforward, however. The very specificity that makes phages so precise also means that treatment must often be tailored to each patient, which sits awkwardly with regulatory systems designed for standardised, mass-produced drugs. Bacteria can also evolve resistance to phages, though researchers hope to counter this by using cocktails of several phages at once or by combining them with antibiotics.

For a handful of drugs, genetic testing before treatment is already standard practice and has prevented dangerous reactions. Crucially, the body appears to react to noise even when the mind has grown accustomed to it. People who insist that they no longer notice the trains passing their bedroom window may still show surges in heart rate and stress hormones each time one goes by. The effects extend to wildlife, too: songbirds in cities sing at higher pitches to make themselves heard, and underwater noise from shipping disrupts the communication of whales. Remedies are well understood, including quieter road surfaces, noise barriers, restrictions on night flights and better insulation of homes, but they compete for funding with problems that seem more urgent, partly because noise leaves no visible trace.

Defunct satellites, discarded rocket stages and countless fragments from explosions and collisions now circle the Earth at speeds of several kilometres per second. At such velocities, even a fragment the size of a coin carries the destructive energy of a hand grenade, posing a serious threat to working satellites and to crewed spacecraft, which must occasionally manoeuvre to avoid passing debris. Scientists have long warned of a cascade effect, in which collisions generate fresh fragments that in turn trigger further collisions, potentially rendering certain orbits unusable for generations. The danger has grown sharply with the deployment of vast constellations of small satellites providing internet access, which are multiplying the number of objects in orbit at an unprecedented rate. Proposed solutions include designing satellites to burn up in the atmosphere at the end of their working lives and developing missions to capture and remove the largest pieces of debris. Progress is hampered, however, by the absence of binding international rules and by an awkward question: who should pay to clean up a mess that nobody admits to owning?

questions.passage: Few psychological ideas have spread as rapidly through schools as the notion of a growth mindset. The theory holds that students who believe intelligence can be developed through effort respond to setbacks more constructively than those who regard it as a fixed trait, and that teaching students the former belief can improve their academic results. Posters exhorting pupils to embrace mistakes appeared in classrooms across many countries, and teachers were encouraged to praise effort rather than talent. As the idea became more popular, however, researchers began to report disappointing results. Some researchers respond by being extremely cautious, publishing transcriptions hedged about with qualifications and declining to perform them at all. Others take a bolder view, arguing that informed guesswork, drawing on surviving instruments, descriptions in literature and comparisons with living traditions, is preferable to silence. Yet they have also attracted large audiences and have sometimes prompted fresh questions that purely textual analysis would never have raised. Novelists have portrayed thirty-year-olds as weary veterans on the brink of death, and popular histories have marvelled at the 'unusual' longevity of figures who in fact lived to quite ordinary ages. Historians do not deny that life was precarious: epidemics, famine and childbirth carried off adults in numbers that would appall us today. A poem's effect depends not merely on what it says but on the sounds of its words, the weight of its rhythms and the associations each term carries in its original culture. None of these survives intact when the words are exchanged for others. Faced with this predicament, translators have adopted strikingly different strategies. Some aim for a literal rendering, often accompanied by notes, on the grounds that readers deserve to know exactly what the original says, even at the cost of music. Others pursue what they call equivalence of effect, freely altering images and even meaning so as to recreate the experience a native reader might have. Still others treat translation as an occasion for a new poem, loosely inspired by the original but frankly their own. Each approach has its partisans and its detractors. What unites the best translators, perhaps, is a refusal to pretend that any version is final. The very impossibility of the task ensures that great poems are translated again and again, each generation finding in them something its predecessors had missed.

A first-person narrator who misleads us, whether deliberately or through self-deception, forces readers into an unusual position: we must attend not only to what is said but to what is being concealed, and we must construct a version of events that the narrator cannot or will not provide. Some critics argue that all narrators are unreliable to some degree, since every account of experience involves selection and interpretation. This is true as far as it goes, but it risks blurring a useful distinction. In most narratives, we are invited to trust the teller, even if we recognise their limitations. In the case of the genuinely unreliable narrator, by contrast, the text actively signals that trust is misplaced, through contradictions, implausible justifications or the reactions of other characters. Reading such works can be an uncomfortable experience, and that discomfort is often the point. By making us complicit in a flawed perspective, these stories expose how easily we, too, accept explanations that flatter our own assumptions.

Should the lost parts be rebuilt exactly as they were, using the original designs and, where possible, traditional methods? Or should any new work be frankly modern, so that visitors can distinguish clearly between what is old and what has been added? Advocates of faithful reconstruction argue that a building is more than a collection of authentic stones; it is a familiar presence in the life of a community, and its loss leaves a wound that only restoration can heal. Their opponents reply that a replica, however skilful, is a kind of forgery, and that pretending the damage never happened falsifies history. In practice, many recent projects have sought a middle path, rebuilding the overall form of a structure while allowing contemporary materials and details to remain visible on closer inspection. Such compromises rarely satisfy purists on either side. Yet they reflect a growing recognition that a building's history includes its injuries, and that the scars of fire or war can themselves become part of what a place means.

questions.passage: The idea that we can know our own minds better than anyone else seems almost too obvious to question. In a series of well-known experiments, participants confidently explained choices they had made, offering reasons that, it later emerged, had played no part in their decisions. They were not lying; they simply constructed plausible stories after the fact and believed them sincerely. Some philosophers conclude from such findings that introspection is far less reliable than we assume, and that our self-knowledge is often a matter of interpretation rather than observation. Others resist this conclusion, noting that the experiments concern explanations of behaviour rather than awareness of sensations or thoughts, where our authority may remain secure. The debate is unresolved. What seems clear, however, is that the inner life is not the transparent glass case of popular imagination, and that a degree of humility about our own motives may be wiser than unexamined confidence.

Supporters respond that opera was never a museum piece in the first place: in its heyday, it was a popular entertainment, performed in noisy theatres where audiences ate, chatted and demanded encores of their favourite arias. A fire did damage part of the collection during a military conflict, but it was neither the first nor the last of the institution's misfortunes. Why, then, does the myth of sudden destruction persist? Part of the answer lies in its narrative power. A dramatic blaze offers a clear villain and a moment of tragedy that a slow decline cannot match. It also carries a moral, warning of the fragility of knowledge in the face of violence. The more prosaic truth may be no less instructive, however. Institutions of learning are seldom destroyed in a single stroke; they are more often eroded by neglect, until one day there is little left to burn.

questions.passage: Dictionaries have traditionally presented themselves as authorities, telling readers how words ought to be spelled, pronounced and used. Their task, as they see it, is to observe how a language is actually employed, drawing on vast databases of real texts, and to report their findings with as little personal judgement as possible. This shift has occasionally provoked outrage. When a respected dictionary acknowledges a meaning that many consider a misuse, critics accuse its editors of surrendering to ignorance. Lexicographers reply that they are merely acknowledging a fact: if millions of speakers use a word in a particular sense, then that sense exists, whether or not anyone approves. They point out, too, that labels such as 'informal' or 'disputed' still give readers guidance about where a usage might cause offence. The dispute reveals a tension in what people want from a dictionary. Many consult one not to learn how language is used, but to settle arguments, and they are disappointed to discover that the book refuses to take sides as firmly as they would wish.

The gradual elevation of landscape to a subject in its own right is one of the more remarkable developments in the history of art. Several factors contributed. Growing towns created a nostalgic appetite for images of the countryside among urban buyers who rarely saw it. Scientific curiosity encouraged closer observation of clouds, rocks and vegetation. Above all, perhaps, a new sensibility emerged that found in nature a source of moral and emotional experience, capable of inspiring awe as profound as any sermon. Painters responded by abandoning the tidy, idealised scenery of their predecessors in favour of storms, mountains and the shifting effects of light. Some even worked outdoors, struggling with wind and changing weather to capture impressions directly. questions.passage: Every language contains words that seem to resist translation, and lists of such terms circulate widely, usually accompanied by the suggestion that their speakers experience the world in uniquely profound ways. A word for the melancholy pleasure of a rainy afternoon, or for the particular embarrassment of forgetting someone's name, is presented as a window into a national soul. Linguists tend to greet these lists with a mixture of amusement and unease. It is true that languages divide experience differently, and that a single word in one may require a whole phrase in another. But the fact that English lacks a word for a feeling hardly means that English speakers cannot have it, or even describe it with precision. Moreover, many supposedly untranslatable terms turn out to be fairly ordinary words whose everyday meaning has been romanticised by enthusiastic compilers. None of this means that comparing vocabularies is pointless. Studied carefully, the ways in which different languages carve up colour, kinship or emotion reveal much about human cognition and culture. The trouble lies in mistaking a lexical gap for a gap in experience.

questions.passage: Classical Greek theatre was a civic event rather than a private pastime. Because the plots were usually drawn from well-known myths, spectators already knew how the stories would end. Suspense, in the modern sense, played little part. What interested the audience was how a particular playwright would handle familiar material, which characters he would sympathise with, and what arguments he would place in their mouths. Comedy, meanwhile, offered a licence for satire that is startling even today, ridiculing politicians by name and mocking the very institutions that sponsored the festival. That a society should fund, and attend in vast numbers, performances so critical of itself says something about the role theatre played in Athenian life. It was less an escape from public affairs than a means of reflecting on them together.

Many alchemists were meticulous experimenters who kept detailed laboratory notebooks, developed techniques for distillation and purification, and accumulated practical knowledge of substances that later chemists would build upon. Some of the most celebrated figures of the scientific revolution devoted considerable effort to alchemical studies, a fact that earlier biographers tended to pass over in embarrassed silence. None of this means that alchemy was simply chemistry under another name. Its practitioners also worked within a framework of spiritual and symbolic ideas that modern science has abandoned, and their writings are often deliberately obscure, intended to be understood only by initiates. The challenge for historians is to resist the temptation either to dismiss alchemy as superstition or to rescue it as proto-science, and instead to understand it on its own terms, as a coherent enterprise with aims of its own.

Some people argue that offending statues should be removed, since their presence in prominent public spaces implies continuing approval. Others warn that taking them down amounts to erasing history, and that it would be better to leave them in place as reminders of the past, however uncomfortable. Between these positions lies a range of alternatives: relocating monuments to museums, adding explanatory plaques, or commissioning new works that respond to the old ones. Historians often point out that the removal of monuments is itself a long-standing historical practice. Regimes have toppled the statues of their predecessors for millennia, and many of the monuments now being contested replaced earlier ones. What is at stake, ultimately, is less the history of the past than the question of how a society chooses to represent itself in the present, and whose stories it decides to place on a pedestal.

questions.passage: The sonnet is one of the most durable forms in European poetry, having survived more than seven centuries of shifting tastes. Its fourteen lines impose severe constraints: a fixed rhyme scheme, a regular metre and, in most traditions, a turn of thought at a prescribed point, where an argument pivots or a mood changes. One might expect such rigidity to stifle creativity, and generations of rebellious poets have duly denounced the form as an artificial straitjacket. Yet the sonnet keeps returning, often in the hands of the very writers who claimed to have outgrown it. Part of its appeal lies precisely in its limitations. A poet who must compress a complex emotion into fourteen lines is forced to choose every word with care, and the tension between the urgency of feeling and the discipline of form can generate extraordinary intensity. Modern poets have also delighted in bending the rules, writing sonnets without rhyme, in fragmented syntax or in colloquial speech, while still relying on readers to recognise the shape they are distorting. The form, it seems, is flexible enough to absorb even the rebellions directed against it.

This image was largely the creation of Renaissance writers themselves, who had every reason to present their own era as a triumphant break with the past. Historians have since dismantled much of it. Medieval scholars, it turns out, had preserved, copied and commented on a great many classical texts, and the universities, cathedral schools and monasteries of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries had witnessed intellectual ferment of their own. Moreover, the cultural achievements associated with the Renaissance were confined to a narrow elite; for most people, daily life changed little. None of this diminishes the genuine brilliance of the artists and thinkers of the period. But it does suggest that the boundaries between historical eras are often drawn by those with an interest in drawing them, and that the labels we inherit can shape our understanding of the past long after their original purpose has been forgotten.

By embedding steel bars within concrete, engineers in the late nineteenth century created a material that combined the compressive strength of stone with the tensile strength of metal, and that could be poured into almost any shape. The consequences were profound. Architects were freed from the need for thick load-bearing walls; floors could cantilever dramatically into space, and roofs could take the form of shells and curves that would have been unthinkable in brick or timber. The material was also cheap and relatively quick to use, which made it indispensable for housing, bridges and infrastructure on a vast scale. Its success has come at a price. The production of cement is responsible for a significant share of global carbon emissions, and concrete structures, once thought to be virtually eternal, have proved vulnerable to corrosion as the steel within them rusts. The material that built the modern world may yet have to be reinvented if that world is to remain habitable.

Performers of long epic poems, it emerged, did not memorise a fixed text; instead, they relied on a repertoire of formulaic phrases, stock scenes and rhythmic patterns that allowed them to recompose the story afresh at each performance. Two versions of the same tale, recorded from the same singer a year apart, might differ considerably in wording while preserving the essential structure and key episodes. From this perspective, the idea of an original or correct version becomes problematic. Each performance is an authentic instance of the tradition, shaped by the occasion, the audience and the mood of the teller. The discovery has had consequences far beyond folklore. It has prompted fresh thinking about some of the oldest works of literature, which may bear the marks of oral composition, and about the relationship between memory, creativity and the written word.

questions.passage: Utilitarianism, in its simplest form, holds that the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number. The theory has an attractive clarity: it promises to settle moral questions by a kind of calculation, setting aside prejudice and tradition in favour of measurable outcomes. Its critics, however, have long pointed to troubling implications. If the only thing that matters is the total amount of well-being, then it might seem permissible, or even obligatory, to sacrifice an innocent individual whenever doing so would benefit enough others. Most people find such conclusions abhorrent, and this reaction is often taken as evidence that the theory leaves something out, perhaps the separateness of persons or the existence of rights that cannot be traded away. Defenders of utilitarianism have responded in various ways. Some bite the bullet, arguing that our intuitions are unreliable and should yield to reasoned principle. Others refine the theory, proposing that we should follow rules which, if generally observed, would tend to maximise happiness, even when breaking them might appear advantageous in a particular case. The debate shows no sign of ending, which is perhaps a measure of how deep the questions run.

Each option has its defenders. Scholars generally favour publication of the raw material, arguing that even an imperfect draft sheds light on how a writer worked. Publishers, mindful of sales, are sometimes tempted by completion, which produces a book that can be marketed to ordinary readers. Executors who knew the author personally may feel bound by private wishes, even when these were never written down. Matters become especially fraught when an author explicitly requested that unpublished papers be destroyed. Literary history contains several celebrated cases in which such instructions were ignored, to the lasting gratitude of readers. Yet it is uncomfortable to build a canon on disobedience. The question ultimately turns on whom a literary work belongs to: the person who wrote it, the heirs who own it, or the readers who, in a sense, bring it to life.

They set prices, controlled the quality of goods, determined who could enter a profession and how long an apprentice had to train before becoming a master. Supporters of the system argued that it protected consumers from shoddy work and craftsmen from ruinous competition. Its critics, then and since, have seen it rather differently, as a cartel designed to keep outsiders out and prices high. Both views contain an element of truth. Guilds did maintain standards and provide a form of social security, supporting members who fell ill and the widows of those who died. At the same time, they could be fiercely exclusive, barring women, foreigners and religious minorities, and resisting technical innovations that threatened established methods. Economists still debate whether guilds hindered or helped economic growth. What is clear is that their decline, which accompanied the rise of industrial production, transformed not only how goods were made but how working lives were organised and protected.

questions.passage: The history of musical instruments is, to a surprising extent, a history of compromise. The modern piano, for example, is tuned according to a system known as equal temperament, in which the octave is divided into twelve identical steps. This arrangement allows a performer to play in any key without retuning, but it comes at a cost: almost every interval is very slightly out of tune compared with the pure ratios that the human ear finds most harmonious. Earlier tuning systems favoured certain keys, making them sound especially sweet, while rendering others so harsh that composers avoided them. The gradual adoption of equal temperament, over roughly two centuries, opened up new possibilities for modulation, enabling composers to move freely between distant keys within a single work. Some musicians regret what was lost in the process, arguing that the distinctive colour of individual keys has been flattened into uniformity. Performers of early music frequently revert to older tunings, and listeners accustomed to modern pianos are often struck by how vivid the results can sound. The episode illustrates a recurring pattern in the arts: gains in flexibility are rarely achieved without some sacrifice of character.

questions.passage: Writing systems are often imagined as having evolved in a single direction, from crude pictures to the efficient alphabets used today. The real story is considerably more tangled. Writing appears to have been invented independently in several parts of the world, and in each case it emerged for practical rather than literary purposes, typically to record goods, debts and taxes. Early scripts combined signs representing whole words with others representing sounds, and many remained mixed systems for thousands of years. The alphabet, in which a relatively small number of letters stand for individual sounds, was a later and comparatively rare development. Its advantages are obvious: it can be learned quickly and adapted easily to new languages. Yet scripts that use thousands of characters have flourished for millennia, and they offer benefits of their own, such as allowing speakers of mutually unintelligible dialects to read the same texts. To regard such systems as primitive stages on the road to an alphabet is to misunderstand them. Each writing system represents a different solution to the problem of making language visible, shaped by the particular structure of the language and the needs of those who used it.

Its adoption by artists in the nineteenth century reflected a conviction that the arts, too, should march in front, challenging convention and leading society towards a new future. For several generations, this self-image proved enormously productive. Movements succeeded one another in rapid succession, each denouncing its predecessor as hopelessly conservative and announcing a radical break with tradition. Exhibitions provoked scandals, manifestos were published with defiant glee, and the shock of the new became a value in itself. Over time, however, a paradox emerged. As museums, collectors and the art market learned to embrace experimental work, the very notion of an avant-garde became difficult to sustain. Works once intended to outrage the establishment were acquired by it for considerable sums, and audiences came to expect provocation as part of the entertainment. Some critics have concluded that the avant-garde is dead, absorbed by the institutions it once opposed. Others argue that its spirit survives in new forms, in practices that operate outside galleries altogether. What has certainly vanished is the confidence that art can stand apart from the society it addresses.

questions.passage: Historians who study daily life in the past face a peculiar problem: the more ordinary an activity was, the less likely anyone was to write about it. Chroniclers recorded battles, coronations and natural disasters, but rarely described how people cooked their meals, washed their clothes or spent their evenings. Such matters were too familiar to seem worth mentioning. To recover them, historians have learned to read sources against the grain. Court records, for instance, though concerned with crimes, often contain incidental details about domestic arrangements, as witnesses explain where they were and what they were doing when an offence occurred. Inventories drawn up after a death list the contents of a household down to the last spoon. Archaeology adds further evidence, from the bones of animals eaten at a particular table to the wear patterns on doorsteps. Assembling these fragments is painstaking work, and the resulting picture inevitably remains partial. Even so, it has transformed our understanding of the past, revealing the routines, anxieties and small pleasures of people who left no memoirs. History, in this view, is not only the record of exceptional events but also the reconstruction of the unremarkable.

A novel can be left unread and a painting ignored, but a building imposes itself on everyone who passes by, whether they wish to look at it or not. This gives architects an unusual responsibility, and it also explains why architectural controversies tend to be so heated. When a striking new tower is proposed for a historic city centre, local residents may object that it will overshadow familiar streets and disrupt a skyline that has defined the place for centuries. Its supporters, meanwhile, argue that cities must evolve, and that many of the buildings now cherished as heritage were themselves bitterly opposed when first erected. Both arguments have force. History offers examples of daring buildings that were reviled at first and later embraced, but it also records many that were simply mistakes, enduring as eyesores for decades. Planning authorities thus find themselves in the unenviable position of trying to predict the verdict of the future. Perhaps the best that can be asked of them is to ensure that the debate is genuinely public, since it is the public who will have to live with the result.

questions.passage: Children acquire their first language with an ease that adults learning a foreign one can only envy. By the age of four or five, most have mastered the basic grammar of their native tongue without any formal instruction, often producing sentences they have never heard before. How they accomplish this feat has been the subject of long-running debate. One influential school holds that humans are born with an innate capacity for language, a set of principles that constrain the kinds of grammar a child will consider. Without such guidance, the argument runs, the input children receive would be far too limited and messy to account for what they eventually know. A rival school places greater emphasis on learning, arguing that children are remarkably skilled at detecting statistical patterns in the speech around them, and that the input is richer than it first appears. Evidence has been marshalled on both sides, and many researchers now suspect that the truth lies somewhere in between. What neither camp disputes is the importance of interaction. Children who are spoken to frequently, and whose attempts at speech receive attentive responses, tend to develop language faster than those who are merely exposed to it.

They began by grinding pigments and preparing panels, progressed to copying drawings, and eventually painted parts of larger works, such as backgrounds, drapery or minor figures, under close supervision. The finished product was often a collaborative effort, though it bore the master's name and reflected his overall design. This system has created headaches for modern scholars and collectors. Attributing a painting to a particular hand is a delicate matter when several hands may have contributed, and the boundary between a work by the master and one by his workshop can be extremely difficult to draw. The financial stakes are considerable, since a painting attributed to a celebrated artist may be worth many times more than one classed as a workshop production. Advances in technical analysis, including infrared imaging that reveals underdrawings, have helped to clarify some cases. Yet they have also complicated others, by showing that even works long accepted as autograph involved assistants. Perhaps the very idea of a single author is, for this period, something of an anachronism.

questions.passage: The relationship between music and mathematics has fascinated thinkers since antiquity. Ancient philosophers observed that strings whose lengths stood in simple ratios produced pleasing intervals, and some concluded that harmony was a reflection of the numerical order underlying the universe itself. The idea proved remarkably persistent, resurfacing in medieval treatises, in the speculations of early astronomers and in modern theories of composition. Yet the connection is easy to overstate. Many people who excel at mathematics have little musical ability, and many fine musicians profess to find numbers baffling. Studies that claim to show that musical training improves mathematical performance have produced mixed results, with effects that often shrink or disappear under rigorous testing. What music and mathematics undoubtedly share is a concern with pattern and structure. A fugue, with its interlocking voices and strict rules of imitation, can be described in terms that would not be out of place in a geometry lesson. But listeners do not experience music as a set of equations. Its power to move us depends on qualities, such as timbre, expectation and memory, that resist reduction to numbers. Structure may be necessary to music, but it is hardly sufficient.

questions.passage: Freedom of the will is one of philosophy's oldest and most intractable problems. On the one hand, we experience ourselves as agents who choose between alternatives, and our practices of praise, blame and punishment presuppose that people could have acted otherwise. On the other hand, the scientific picture of the world suggests that every event, including every decision, is the product of prior causes. If my choices are determined by my genes, my upbringing and the state of my brain, in what sense are they truly mine? Some philosophers, known as incompatibilists, conclude that if determinism is true, free will is an illusion. Others, called compatibilists, argue that freedom does not require escaping causation altogether. On their view, an action is free if it flows from the agent's own desires and reasoning, rather than from external compulsion, even if those desires themselves have causes. Critics complain that this redefinition changes the subject, offering a diluted freedom in place of the real thing. Compatibilists retort that the 'real thing' their opponents demand is incoherent, since an action produced by nothing at all would be random rather than free. The argument, after more than two thousand years, continues.

questions.passage: The detective story is often regarded as a light entertainment, but its emergence in the nineteenth century reflected profound social changes. Rapidly growing cities had made anonymity a common experience: people lived among strangers whose histories they did not know, and crime could flourish in the gaps between them. At the same time, the establishment of professional police forces and the growing prestige of science encouraged the belief that mysteries could be solved by careful observation and logical deduction. The fictional detective embodied this faith. Typically an outsider, often eccentric, he restored order by reading clues that others overlooked, transforming the chaotic city into a legible text. Readers found the formula deeply reassuring. However disturbing the crime, the final chapter would explain everything and identify the culprit. Later writers have frequently subverted these conventions, producing stories in which the detective fails, the solution remains ambiguous or the investigator turns out to be compromised. Such works reflect a diminished confidence in the power of reason to make sense of the modern world. That the classic formula remains enormously popular, nonetheless, suggests that the desire for reassurance has not disappeared.

The perspectives of colonised peoples, when they appeared at all, were filtered through the eyes of officials who often misunderstood them. Recovering those perspectives presents formidable challenges. Many communities left few written records, and those that existed were sometimes deliberately destroyed. Historians have therefore drawn on oral testimony, songs, petitions, and the marginal notes and complaints that occasionally surface in official files. They have also learned to read colonial documents with scepticism, attending to what officials feared, ignored or failed to understand. The resulting histories are often more complicated than earlier narratives of imposition and resistance. They reveal accommodation as well as defiance, divisions within colonised societies, and the many ways in which ordinary people negotiated, exploited or evaded the systems imposed upon them. The aim is not to replace one simplification with another, but to restore complexity to the past.

What the gardener seeks is not a copy of nature but an essence, a landscape distilled to its most evocative elements. Some gardens are designed to be viewed from a single vantage point, such as the veranda of a temple, while others reveal themselves gradually as visitors follow a winding path, each turn disclosing a carefully composed view. Techniques such as 'borrowed scenery', in which distant hills or trees beyond the garden wall are incorporated into the composition, blur the boundary between the cultivated and the wild. Visitors from other traditions sometimes find these gardens austere, missing the abundance of flowers they associate with the word 'garden'. Yet their restraint is precisely the point. By eliminating the superfluous, the designer invites contemplation, encouraging the viewer to notice the texture of moss, the play of shadow and the slow passage of the seasons.

Its elevation was a matter of social power rather than linguistic merit. Once established, the standard was codified in grammars and dictionaries, taught in schools and used in official documents, while other varieties were increasingly labelled as rustic, incorrect or uneducated. Speakers of those varieties often internalised the stigma, abandoning their native speech in public or feeling ashamed of it. Linguists insist that every dialect possesses a systematic grammar and is fully capable of expressing complex ideas. Features that are dismissed as errors, such as double negatives, are in many cases perfectly regular and have parallels in the standard forms of other languages. This is not to deny the practical value of a shared standard, which allows people from different regions to communicate in writing and in formal settings. The point is to recognise that its authority is a social convention, not a law of nature.

If a composer wrote a mournful symphony shortly after a bereavement, it seems natural to hear the music as an expression of grief; if a painter's palette darkened in old age, the change is readily attributed to illness or disappointment. Such interpretations can be illuminating, but they also carry risks. Artists frequently produced cheerful works during periods of personal misery and sombre ones when their lives were going well. Commissions, deadlines and the conventions of a genre often shaped a work more decisively than the creator's mood. Moreover, the biographical approach can encourage a circular kind of reasoning, in which the life is reconstructed from the works and then used to explain them. Some critics have reacted by insisting that a work should be judged entirely on its own terms, without reference to its maker. This position, too, has its limits, since knowledge of an artist's circumstances can reveal allusions and meanings that would otherwise be missed. To modern sensibilities this may seem absurd, yet it reflected a widespread taste for melancholy reflection. A ruin invited the viewer to meditate on the passage of time, the vanity of human ambition and the inevitable decline of empires, themes that resonated with an age anxious about its own place in history. Painters depicted ruins overgrown with vegetation, emphasising nature's slow triumph over human effort, while poets mused on the fates of forgotten kings. The taste for ruins also had a political edge. Collectors who travelled the countryside in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries to record such songs were not neutral observers, either. They frequently selected the material that matched their own ideas of what was authentic, ignoring popular songs they considered vulgar, and they sometimes tidied up words they found indelicate. Their published collections thus shaped the very tradition they claimed merely to document. None of this means that folk song is a fraud. Songs genuinely did circulate by ear, and singers did adapt them freely, adding verses, altering melodies and fitting them to local circumstances. But the notion of a pure tradition, untouched by commerce or by educated intervention, is itself something of a romantic invention. The history of folk music, like most histories, is a story of exchange, borrowing and reinvention.

The ancient Stoics embedded their advice within a comprehensive account of the universe as a rational order and of human beings as citizens of a world community, with duties extending far beyond personal well-being. Previously, most professional musicians had been employed by churches, courts or aristocratic households, composing and performing for patrons whose tastes they were obliged to satisfy. The emergence of concerts open to anyone who could buy a ticket created a new kind of public, anonymous and commercially minded, whose approval could make or break a reputation. Composers responded by writing works designed to impress large audiences in sizeable halls, and virtuoso performers began to cultivate personal fame through touring. The shift brought new freedoms. A composer who could attract paying listeners was no longer wholly dependent on the whims of a single employer. Yet it also introduced new pressures, as success now hinged on the unpredictable preferences of the market. Some musicians thrived in this environment; others struggled to make a living, and the image of the impoverished, misunderstood genius dates largely from this period. The modern music industry, with its blend of artistic ambition and commercial calculation, has its roots in these developments, and many of its tensions would have been familiar to musicians of that age.

questions.passage: For decades, economists assumed that a modest rise in the minimum wage would inevitably price the least skilled workers out of a job. The logic seemed watertight: make labour dearer, and employers will buy less of it. Yet a growing body of fieldwork has complicated that tidy picture. When neighbouring regions with different wage floors were compared, employment in low-paid sectors often barely moved, and in some cases it actually edged upwards. One explanation lies in what economists call monopsony power. Where a handful of firms dominate local hiring, they can keep pay below what workers would earn in a genuinely competitive market, and a higher legal minimum merely claws back part of that gap. Higher pay also tends to reduce staff turnover, sparing employers the considerable expense of constantly recruiting and training newcomers. None of this means the floor can be raised indefinitely without consequence; beyond a certain point, the textbook warnings would surely reassert themselves. The real dispute, then, is no longer whether minimum wages destroy jobs in principle, but where, in any given economy, that tipping point happens to lie.

Its defenders prize the clarity this produces: governments are usually formed by a single party, and voters know exactly whom to blame when things go wrong. Critics retort that it routinely manufactures majorities out of minorities, leaving millions of votes with no bearing whatsoever on the outcome. Proportional systems, by contrast, allocate seats roughly in line with each party's share of the national vote. Parliaments thus mirror the electorate more faithfully, but coalition governments become the norm, and the bargaining that follows an election can drag on for months. Smaller parties may find themselves wielding influence out of all proportion to their support, precisely because larger partners cannot govern without them. There is, in short, no neutral option: every system embodies a judgement about whether accountability or representativeness ought to take priority.
