questions.passage: Burnout has become one of the defining complaints of contemporary working life, yet the term is frequently misunderstood. It does not simply mean feeling tired after a demanding week. Psychologists describe it as a state of chronic exhaustion accompanied by growing cynicism towards one's job and a corrosive sense that nothing one does makes any difference. Because it is so often framed as a personal failing, the conventional remedies tend to focus on the individual: meditation apps, wellness seminars and advice to set firmer boundaries. Such measures may help at the margins, but research points to deeper causes rooted in the organisation of work itself. Employees are most at risk when demands are relentless, control over their work is minimal, effort goes unrecognised and the values of the organisation clash with their own. A nurse expected to deliver compassionate care while rushing between far too many patients is unlikely to be rescued by a breathing exercise. Tackling burnout seriously, therefore, means examining workloads, staffing levels and decision-making structures, which is considerably less comfortable for employers than offering a free subscription to a relaxation app.

questions.passage: Lobbying suffers from a lamentable reputation, conjuring images of shadowy figures trading favours in hotel bars. Yet in principle it is an unremarkable, even necessary, part of democratic life. Legislators cannot possibly master the technical details of every industry they regulate, and they depend on information from those affected, whether companies, trade unions or charities. The problem lies not in lobbying as such but in the inequality of access it can entrench. A multinational corporation can afford teams of specialists, glossy reports and a steady stream of invitations to dinners and conferences; a group of local residents objecting to a new development can rarely match such resources. When the same voices are heard again and again, policy can drift towards the interests of the well-funded without any single act of corruption ever taking place. Reformers have proposed various remedies, including public registers listing every meeting between officials and lobbyists, limits on gifts and hospitality, and 'cooling-off' periods preventing former ministers from immediately joining firms they once regulated. Transparency alone cannot equalise influence, but it at least allows citizens to see who is whispering in whose ear.

questions.passage: Jury service is one of the few civic duties that ordinary citizens may be compelled to perform, and one of the most demanding. Twelve strangers, with no legal training, are asked to sit through days or weeks of evidence, some of it highly technical, and to reach a verdict that may change a defendant's life forever. Critics sometimes question whether laypeople are equipped for such a task, particularly in complex fraud cases involving bewildering financial transactions. Some have proposed that such trials be heard by judges alone. Defenders of the jury, however, maintain that its value lies precisely in its amateur status. Jurors bring the common sense and varied experience of the community into the courtroom, acting as a check on the possibility that professional judges might grow jaded or too closely aligned with the state. Research into jury deliberations, though restricted in many countries by rules protecting their secrecy, suggests that jurors generally take their responsibility extremely seriously and pool their recollections to compensate for individual lapses of memory. Their weakness, if any, lies less in a lack of diligence than in the clarity of the instructions they receive.

questions.passage: University tuition fees have provoked fierce argument wherever they have been introduced or raised. Supporters contend that graduates, who typically earn more over their lifetimes than those without degrees, should bear a share of the cost of the education from which they personally benefit, rather than leaving the entire bill to taxpayers, many of whom never attended university themselves. Opponents counter that education yields broad social benefits, from a more productive economy to a better-informed citizenry, and should therefore be funded collectively. They also fear that the prospect of substantial debt will deter talented students from poorer backgrounds. The evidence on that last point is mixed. In some systems, where repayments are linked to income and written off after a certain number of years, participation among disadvantaged groups has continued to rise. In such cases the so-called debt resembles a graduate tax more than a conventional loan. Even so, perceptions matter as much as financial realities. A teenager who hears that university will leave them owing a five-figure sum may simply decide it is not for them, however favourable the actual repayment terms might be.

questions.passage: Megacities, conurbations of more than ten million people, were once a rarity confined to a few industrial powers. Today they are scattered across every inhabited continent, and most of the newest are located in the developing world. Their growth has frequently outpaced any attempt to plan it. Migrants arriving from the countryside in search of work often settle in informal settlements on the urban fringe, building homes from whatever materials are available, on land to which they hold no legal title. Such neighbourhoods are often portrayed simply as zones of deprivation, and many indeed lack clean water, sanitation and secure housing. Yet this portrayal overlooks their remarkable dynamism. Informal settlements frequently host thriving networks of small businesses, mutual support and self-organised services, and they offer newcomers a first foothold in the urban economy. Attempts to clear them wholesale have tended to destroy these networks while scattering residents to even more precarious locations. A growing number of governments have therefore turned to upgrading instead, granting residents secure tenure and gradually installing infrastructure, so that settlements can improve themselves without being uprooted.

questions.passage: The guidebook, once an indispensable companion for any traveller, has been steadily displaced by smartphones, review sites and the endless scroll of social media. The change has brought undeniable conveniences. Travellers can now check opening hours in seconds, read thousands of opinions about a restaurant before choosing it, and navigate unfamiliar streets without unfolding a single map. Yet some observers detect a subtle loss in the bargain. Ratings and algorithms tend to funnel visitors towards the same handful of highly rated places, so that a café praised online may be overwhelmed while a perfectly good establishment around the corner sits empty. Photographs shared widely online can also turn obscure viewpoints into crowded queues of people waiting to reproduce an identical image. Perhaps most significantly, constant connectivity reduces the scope for serendipity, the happy accident of stumbling upon something unplanned. Earlier generations of travellers, armed only with a battered book and a phrasebook, were frequently forced to ask locals for directions and recommendations, and those encounters often became the most memorable part of a journey. Convenience, in this case, may come at the price of discovery.

questions.passage: Doping scandals have a dispiriting habit of recurring. Each new revelation is greeted with expressions of shock, solemn promises of reform and a fresh round of testing, only for the cycle to begin again a few years later. Part of the difficulty is that the incentives remain overwhelming. For an athlete at the margins of elite competition, the difference between winning and finishing fourth can mean the difference between lucrative sponsorship and obscurity, and the temptation to seek an illicit advantage is correspondingly strong. Testers, meanwhile, are perpetually playing catch-up, as new substances and methods are developed specifically to evade detection. One response has been the introduction of biological passports, which track an athlete's physiological markers over time rather than searching for a particular drug. Suspicious fluctuations can thus reveal manipulation even when the substance itself remains unidentified. Stored samples, moreover, can now be retested years later using improved techniques, and several champions have been stripped of medals long after their careers ended. Deterrence, in other words, depends less on catching every cheat immediately than on making sure that no one can ever feel entirely safe.

questions.passage: Few foods have been subjected to such dramatic swings in public opinion as fat. For much of the late twentieth century, dietary advice cast it as the principal villain, and supermarket shelves filled with low-fat versions of everything from yoghurt to biscuits. What received less attention was that many of these products compensated for the loss of flavour and texture by adding sugar and refined starches. As evidence accumulated, nutritionists began to revise their earlier certainties. Not all fats, it emerged, are alike: those found in olive oil, nuts and oily fish appear to be beneficial, whereas certain industrially produced fats are clearly harmful. The pendulum then swung so far that some popular diets began to celebrate fat while demonising carbohydrates with equal zeal. Most researchers regard this as another oversimplification. The more robust finding, repeated across numerous studies, is that diets built around minimally processed foods tend to be healthier than those dominated by heavily processed products, whatever their precise balance of nutrients. The persistent search for a single dietary culprit, it seems, says more about our appetite for simple stories than about the science.

questions.passage: Volunteering is often celebrated as the purest expression of civic spirit, and its contribution to society is immense. Food banks, youth clubs, sports teams and mountain rescue services would struggle to exist without people prepared to give their time for nothing. Yet patterns of volunteering are shifting in ways that worry many organisations. The traditional volunteer, who committed to the same role every week for years, is becoming rarer. Busier working lives, caring responsibilities and greater mobility have made long-term commitments harder to sustain. In their place has emerged a more episodic style of participation, in which people contribute intensively for a single event or project and then move on. Organisations that rely on continuity, such as befriending services for isolated older people, find this trend particularly challenging. Some charities have adapted by breaking roles into smaller tasks that can be completed flexibly or remotely. There is a further concern: surveys suggest that formal volunteering is concentrated among the better-off and better-educated, partly because they have more time and confidence. Widening participation may thus require removing practical barriers, such as reimbursing travel costs, rather than merely appealing to goodwill.

questions.passage: Globalisation was long presented as an almost irresistible force, a tide of trade, investment and supply chains that would continue to rise indefinitely. Recent years have tested that assumption. A series of shocks, including a pandemic that halted factories and a succession of geopolitical disputes, exposed the fragility of supply chains stretched across continents. Companies that had pursued efficiency above all else, holding minimal stocks and relying on a single overseas supplier, discovered how quickly a disruption in one place could paralyse production elsewhere. Many have since begun to diversify, adding suppliers in different countries or bringing some manufacturing closer to home. Governments, too, have become more willing to subsidise strategic industries such as semiconductors and pharmaceuticals. Talk of 'deglobalisation', however, may be premature. Trade volumes remain high, and the reorganisation under way looks more like a reshuffling than a retreat: supply chains are being redrawn along lines of political trust rather than dismantled altogether. The new priority is resilience, even if that means accepting somewhat higher costs, a trade-off that consumers may ultimately notice in the prices they pay.

Strictly speaking, most trials have not compressed five days of work into four longer ones; instead, staff have kept their full salaries while working around eighty per cent of their previous hours, on the understanding that output would be maintained. The results reported so far have been striking. Many participating firms observed little or no decline in productivity, alongside marked reductions in sick leave and staff turnover, and the majority chose to continue the arrangement after the trial ended. Sceptics urge caution before drawing sweeping conclusions. The organisations that volunteered for such trials were presumably those most confident that the model would suit them, and many were small firms in office-based sectors. Whether the same gains could be achieved in hospitals, schools or factories, where output is closely tied to the hours staff are physically present, remains far less certain. In such settings, a shorter week might require hiring additional staff, raising costs considerably. The debate, then, is shifting from whether a four-day week can work to where and for whom.

questions.passage: Referendums possess an undeniable democratic appeal. Rather than entrusting a momentous decision to elected representatives, they allow citizens to settle it directly, and their results carry a legitimacy that few parliamentary votes can match. Yet the device is more problematic than its simplicity suggests. Complex questions, involving countless legal, economic and diplomatic details, must be reduced to a binary choice, and voters are frequently asked to approve or reject a proposal whose consequences no one can fully foresee. Campaigns may focus less on the question itself than on the popularity of the government that called the vote, transforming a constitutional decision into a verdict on a particular leader. There is also the question of permanence. Unlike an election, which can be reversed a few years later, a referendum is often treated as final, even when the result was narrow and circumstances subsequently change. Some democracies attempt to mitigate these difficulties by requiring a minimum turnout or a qualified majority for constitutional changes, or by holding a second confirmatory vote once the details are known. Such safeguards are themselves contested, however, since critics regard them as moving the goalposts after the people have spoken.

questions.passage: Intellectual property law attempts to balance two competing goods. On the one hand, inventors, writers and artists need some assurance that others will not simply copy their work the moment it appears; otherwise, the incentive to invest time and money in creation would be severely weakened. On the other, ideas and culture flourish through borrowing, adaptation and reinterpretation, and granting creators perpetual control would stifle the very creativity the law seeks to encourage. The compromise has traditionally been a limited monopoly: patents and copyrights confer exclusive rights for a fixed period, after which the work enters the public domain and may be used freely by anyone. Over the past century, however, copyright terms in many countries have been extended repeatedly, often lasting for decades after the creator's death. Critics argue that these extensions benefit large corporations holding valuable catalogues far more than living artists, and that they lock away vast quantities of material whose owners can no longer even be traced. Such orphan works cannot legally be digitised or republished, leaving libraries and archives unable to share a substantial portion of the twentieth century's cultural output.

questions.passage: Grade inflation, the gradual rise in the proportion of students awarded top marks, has become a recurring source of anxiety in schools and universities alike. Each year brings headlines lamenting that an excellent grade no longer means what it once did. Defenders of rising results insist that they reflect genuine improvements: better teaching, more focused preparation and students who work harder than their predecessors. There may be some truth in this, yet it is difficult to dismiss the suspicion that other pressures are at work. Institutions judged by league tables have an obvious interest in generous marking, and universities competing for fee-paying students may be reluctant to award grades that could deter applicants. Whatever its causes, inflation erodes the usefulness of grades as signals. When a large share of candidates obtain the highest classification, employers and admissions tutors can no longer distinguish the exceptional from the merely very good, and they turn instead to other criteria, such as interviews, aptitude tests or, less fairly, the prestige of the institution attended. Ironically, then, generous marking may end up disadvantaging the very students it appears to reward, especially those from less renowned schools.

questions.passage: Gentrification is one of the most emotionally charged words in urban debate. It describes the process by which wealthier newcomers move into a working-class neighbourhood, often attracted by low rents and characterful old buildings, and gradually transform its character. Cafés and galleries replace hardware shops and launderettes; property values climb; and long-standing residents may find themselves priced out of the streets where they grew up. Yet the phenomenon resists simple moral judgements. Investment can bring welcome improvements, from renovated housing to safer streets and better-stocked shops, and some original residents, particularly homeowners, benefit considerably from rising values. Studies tracking individual households have also found that displacement, though real and painful, is sometimes less widespread than popular accounts imply, as many tenants remain in place for years. The deeper problem may be that cities rarely build enough affordable housing to absorb rising demand, so that any desirable neighbourhood becomes a battleground. Measures such as protecting tenants from sudden evictions, requiring new developments to include affordable units and supporting community land trusts may soften the effects without freezing a neighbourhood in time.

Passengers have learned to navigate a bewildering array of optional charges, and the advertised fare frequently bears only a passing resemblance to the final bill. Consumer groups have campaigned for clearer pricing, and regulators in several countries now require that unavoidable charges be included in the headline fare. The broader consequences are harder to assess. Cheap flights have opened up travel to people who could previously never have afforded it and have revitalised some provincial economies. Research on elite athletes, however, paints a more nuanced picture. Many who reached the very top sampled a variety of sports throughout childhood and committed to one only in their mid-teens. This broader early experience appears to develop a wider range of movement skills, which can later be transferred to the chosen discipline. Early specialisers, by contrast, are disproportionately prone to overuse injuries, as the same muscles and joints are subjected to repetitive strain while the body is still growing. They are also more likely to suffer from burnout and to abandon sport altogether before reaching adulthood. There are exceptions, notably in disciplines such as gymnastics, where peak performance arrives unusually young. For most sports, though, the evidence suggests that encouraging children to play widely and for enjoyment is not merely kinder but may also produce better athletes in the long run.

Producing cells at scale requires nutrient-rich growth media that remain expensive, and replicating the texture of a steak, with its intricate structure of muscle and fat, is far harder than producing minced meat. The environmental benefits, too, depend heavily on the source of the energy used in production; powered by fossil fuels, the process could prove less green than its promoters suggest. Then there is the question of public acceptance. Surveys show considerable curiosity but also unease about food perceived as unnatural, and several governments have moved to restrict sales or labelling, sometimes under pressure from farming lobbies. Whether cultivated meat becomes a staple or remains a costly novelty may depend as much on politics and perception as on any technical breakthrough.

Falling birth rates combined with rising life expectancy mean that the proportion of people over sixty-five is climbing steadily, while the share of working age is shrinking. Commentators frequently describe this as a demographic time bomb, warning that fewer workers will have to support ever more pensioners through taxes and contributions. Such alarm contains a kernel of truth: pension and healthcare systems designed for younger populations will undoubtedly come under strain. Yet the metaphor can obscure as much as it reveals. Older people today are, on average, healthier than previous generations at the same age, and many wish to continue working, volunteering or caring for grandchildren, contributions that conventional statistics tend to overlook. Raising the retirement age gradually, enabling flexible work for older employees and encouraging migration of working-age adults are among the policy responses available. Each, admittedly, carries political costs, and none can be implemented overnight. The underlying point, however, is that ageing is a challenge to be managed rather than a catastrophe to be awaited, and that its consequences depend heavily on choices that societies have yet to make.

Behavioural economists have spent decades documenting the many ways in which real human beings fall short of this ideal. We procrastinate, overvalue immediate rewards, follow the crowd and are swayed by the way choices are framed. A surgical procedure described as having a ninety per cent survival rate is far more appealing than one described as having a ten per cent mortality rate, even though the information is identical. Governments have seized on such findings to design so-called nudges, which steer behaviour without restricting choice. Enrolling employees in a pension scheme automatically, while allowing them to opt out, has substantially raised saving rates, since most people simply stick with whatever option is presented as the default. Critics, however, raise two objections. Some argue that nudging is subtly manipulative, exploiting cognitive weaknesses rather than persuading people openly. Others contend that its effects are often modest, and that a fondness for cheap behavioural tweaks may distract policymakers from tackling deeper structural problems that require more costly intervention.

questions.passage: Automation has stoked fears about the future of work for as long as machines have existed. Nineteenth-century weavers smashed the looms they believed would destroy their livelihoods, and every subsequent wave of technology has revived similar anxieties. History offers some reassurance: although particular occupations vanished, new ones emerged that no one could have predicted, and overall employment continued to grow. Yet economists caution against assuming that the pattern will automatically repeat itself. The latest generation of software can perform tasks once thought to require human judgement, such as drafting documents, analysing images and answering customer queries, and it is spreading far faster than the steam engine ever did. What seems most likely, at least in the short term, is not the wholesale disappearance of jobs but their transformation. Most occupations consist of bundles of tasks, some of which can be automated while others cannot. An accountant may spend less time reconciling figures and more time advising clients. The transition, however, is unlikely to be painless, and its costs tend to fall on workers whose skills are suddenly devalued and who lack the means to retrain.

questions.passage: Proposals to lower the voting age to sixteen have gained ground in several democracies, and a handful have already implemented them, at least for local or regional elections. Advocates point out that sixteen-year-olds may work, pay taxes and, in some countries, marry, and that it seems inconsistent to deny them a say in how they are governed. They also argue that young people will live longest with the consequences of today's decisions on matters such as climate and public debt. Opponents question whether teenagers possess sufficient maturity and knowledge, and some suspect that the proposal is promoted by parties expecting to benefit from younger voters. Evidence from places that have made the change offers intriguing insights. Turnout among sixteen- and seventeen-year-olds has often been higher than among those aged eighteen to twenty-four, possibly because younger voters still live at home and are encouraged by their families and schools to participate. Voting early, moreover, appears to foster a lasting habit. If so, lowering the voting age might do more than enfranchise a small group; it could help reverse the long decline in electoral participation.

questions.passage: Conventional criminal justice is largely concerned with determining guilt and imposing punishment. The victim, in this model, is often reduced to a witness, while the offender rarely confronts the human consequences of the crime. Restorative justice approaches the matter from a different angle. Where both parties agree, it brings victims and offenders together, usually with a trained facilitator, to discuss what happened, how it affected those involved and what might be done to repair the harm. For many victims, the opportunity to ask questions and describe their experience directly proves remarkably valuable, easing fear and anger in a way that a courtroom verdict seldom does. Offenders, meanwhile, are confronted with the reality of their actions rather than an abstract sentence. Studies suggest that such programmes can modestly reduce reoffending and generally leave victims more satisfied than conventional proceedings. Restorative justice is not, however, a soft alternative suitable for every case. Participation must be entirely voluntary, and in situations involving severe violence or an ongoing imbalance of power, such as domestic abuse, practitioners warn that a face-to-face meeting could cause further harm rather than healing.

Yet they have often been treated by authorities primarily as a problem of public order, to be policed and restricted rather than nurtured. Residents complain, understandably, about noise, litter and rowdy crowds, and many cities responded over the years by tightening licensing rules and shortening opening hours. A number of venues closed as a result, compounded by rising rents and redevelopment pressures. The loss of small music venues proved particularly damaging, since they serve as the training ground where emerging artists hone their craft. In recent years, several cities have adopted a more balanced approach, appointing officials sometimes nicknamed 'night mayors' to mediate between businesses, residents and the police. Policies such as the 'agent of change' principle, which requires the developer of new flats next to an existing venue to pay for soundproofing, have helped prevent established clubs from being forced out by newcomers who knowingly moved in next door. The aim is not to abolish conflict, which is inevitable, but to manage it intelligently.

questions.passage: Home advantage is among the most robust phenomena in sport. Across football, basketball, rugby and many other games, teams win noticeably more often on their own ground than away from it. Explanations have traditionally centred on the crowd, whose roar is thought to lift the home players and intimidate their opponents, but researchers have long suspected that the effect operates partly through officials. Referees, after all, are human, and the pressure of tens of thousands of partisan spectators may subtly influence close decisions on fouls, penalties and added time. An unexpected natural experiment arose when matches were played behind closed doors during the pandemic. In several leagues, home advantage shrank markedly, and the imbalance in fouls and cards awarded to visiting teams largely disappeared. Other factors cannot be ruled out entirely. Familiarity with the pitch, the absence of tiring travel and even territorial instincts may each play a part, which helps explain why home advantage did not vanish altogether. Nevertheless, the empty stadiums provided persuasive evidence that a significant portion of the advantage owes less to inspired players than to the influence of the crowd on those who officiate.

questions.passage: Street food occupies a curious position in many cities. It is celebrated in travel programmes and guidebooks as the authentic taste of a place, and visitors queue eagerly at stalls selling dumplings, grilled skewers or freshly fried pastries. Yet the vendors themselves often operate in a legal grey zone, subject to harassment, confiscation and sudden eviction by authorities who regard them as a hygiene risk or an obstacle to modernisation. For millions of people, particularly in rapidly growing cities, street food is far more than a tourist attraction. It provides affordable nourishment for workers who cannot afford restaurants and lack time or space to cook, and it offers a livelihood, often to women and recent migrants, requiring little initial capital. Some cities have attempted to reconcile these interests by relocating vendors into purpose-built food centres equipped with running water and proper waste disposal. Where such schemes are well designed and centrally located, they have raised standards while preserving livelihoods. Where vendors are moved to remote sites far from their customers, however, the result has often been the collapse of businesses that had flourished for decades.

When a billionaire's foundation commands resources greater than the budgets of many governments, its priorities can shape entire fields of research or national education policies, without the accountability to which elected officials are subject. Critics also note that charitable donations are often tax-deductible, meaning that the public effectively subsidises causes chosen by private individuals, who may favour the institutions they themselves attended or the arts they enjoy over less glamorous needs. Defenders counter that philanthropists can take risks that governments, wary of public criticism, rarely dare to take, funding unconventional ideas that sometimes produce extraordinary breakthroughs. Some donors have responded to the criticism by committing to greater transparency, consulting the communities they aim to help, and pledging to give away most of their wealth within their lifetimes. Whether such measures adequately address concerns about democratic accountability remains, unsurprisingly, a matter of considerable dispute.

questions.passage: Rent control is one of the rare policies on which most economists agree, and their verdict is largely unfavourable. Capping the rent landlords can charge, they argue, may help existing tenants in the short term, but over time it discourages investment in new housing and the maintenance of old, as owners find the returns insufficient. Some landlords convert their properties into owner-occupied flats or short-term holiday lets, further reducing the supply available to renters. The beneficiaries, moreover, are not necessarily those in greatest need: a well-paid professional who happens to occupy a controlled flat gains just as much as a struggling family, and tenants become reluctant to move even when their circumstances change. Supporters of rent regulation reply that the textbook model ignores the realities of tight housing markets, in which tenants have little bargaining power and sudden rent rises can uproot families, disrupting children's schooling and fragmenting communities. Many now favour more moderate forms of regulation, such as limiting how quickly rents can rise within an existing tenancy, while leaving initial rents to the market. Such measures aim to provide stability without choking off the construction that ultimately determines affordability.

questions.passage: Bilingual education was once viewed with considerable suspicion. Well into the twentieth century, many educators believed that exposing children to two languages would confuse them, slow their development and hinder their mastery of the dominant language. In some countries, pupils were even punished for speaking their home language at school. Research has since overturned much of this thinking. Children are capable of acquiring two or more languages simultaneously, and although bilingual infants may initially have a slightly smaller vocabulary in each language, their combined vocabulary is typically comparable to that of monolingual peers, and any lag generally disappears within a few years. Claims that bilingualism confers broad cognitive advantages, such as superior attention or problem-solving, have proved more contentious, with some studies failing to replicate earlier findings. The strongest arguments for bilingual education may therefore lie elsewhere. Maintaining a home language allows children to communicate with grandparents and relatives, preserves cultural identity and keeps open opportunities in a globalised labour market. Programmes that build on what children already know, rather than demanding that they abandon it, also tend to produce better results in the majority language itself.

questions.passage: Few experiences reveal the hidden architecture of everyday life as starkly as travelling across time zones. Within hours, a traveller can be transported to a place where the sun rises when their body expects midnight, and the internal clock that regulates sleep, hunger and alertness struggles to adjust. The resulting jet lag is far more than mere tiredness. It can disturb digestion, impair concentration and dull judgement for several days, which is why some sports teams arrive at distant tournaments well in advance and some companies discourage executives from signing contracts on the day they land. Curiously, the direction of travel matters. Most people find flying east considerably more taxing than flying west, because it requires the body to advance its clock, going to sleep earlier than it wishes, whereas the natural tendency of the human rhythm is to drift slightly later each day. Exposure to daylight at the right times remains the most effective remedy, helping the internal clock to reset, while carefully timed naps and meals offer modest assistance. Remedies promising instant relief, by contrast, are rarely supported by convincing evidence.

Those who remember the voyages speak of a rhythm that no flight can reproduce: days at sea, deck chairs, formal dinners and the slow dawning of a distant coastline. Nostalgia for this lost world sustains a small trade in memorabilia, and the few liners still crossing are booked months in advance by those who want to arrive slowly.

items.q: What replaced ocean liners for Atlantic crossings?
What happened to the liners?
options: They were converted into cruise vessels or scrapped
They were sold to the navy

items.q: Who books the remaining liners?
options: Those who want to arrive slowly

questions.explanation: The text says hungry shoppers "buy more, and more high-calorie food", supermarkets place displays "near entrances", and the defence is "a list and a snack beforehand".
questions.passage: The conventional wisdom that one should never go shopping when hungry has a basis in research. Studies show that people who shop on an empty stomach buy more, and more high-calorie food, than those who have eaten. The explanation lies partly in physiology, since hunger heightens the appeal of immediate rewards, and partly in psychology, as the sight of food prompts imagined pleasure. Supermarkets, aware of this, place enticing displays near entrances and tempting smells near the bakery. The simplest defence, shoppers find, is a list and a snack beforehand; both, apparently, are more effective than willpower.

items.q: What do people who shop hungry buy?
Where do supermarkets place enticing displays?
What is the simplest defence?
options: A list and a snack beforehand

questions.explanation: The text says "work, families and geography conspire against sustained closeness", surviving friendships are "sustained by small gestures", and "friendship is less a matter of chemistry than of effort".
questions.passage: Friendship in adulthood is often more fragile than we care to admit. In youth, shared circumstances such as school or university provide ready-made opportunities for contact; later, work, families and geography conspire against sustained closeness. Surveys indicate that many people report having fewer close friends than they did a decade earlier, and that men in particular are prone to isolation. Yet friendships that survive tend to be remarkably resilient, sustained by small gestures: a message at the right moment, a visit that costs inconvenience. The lesson, such research suggests, is that friendship is less a matter of chemistry than of effort, and that effort once withdrawn is difficult to restore.

items.q: Why is adult friendship fragile?
options: Work, family and geography make contact harder

items.q: What sustains friendships that survive?
What is the lesson drawn?
options: Friendship depends on effort, which is hard to restore once withdrawn

questions.explanation: The text says change "destroy[s] some occupations while creating others", optimists say routine tasks go while "creativity, judgment and empathy" remain, and the third view asks "who will own the machines".
questions.passage: The rise of automation has revived an old fear that machines will make human labour redundant. Historically, however, technological change has tended to destroy some occupations while creating others, and overall employment has not fallen. Optimists point out that the tasks most easily automated are routine ones, leaving people free to concentrate on work requiring creativity, judgment and empathy. Pessimists counter that the pace of current change is unprecedented, and that displaced workers cannot be expected to retrain overnight. A third view holds that the central question is not how many jobs will exist but who will own the machines, and therefore who will capture the gains.

items.q: What has historically happened with technological change?
options: Some jobs were destroyed while others were created

items.q: What do optimists argue?
options: Routine tasks will be automated, leaving creative work to people

items.q: What does the third view emphasise?
options: Who owns the machines and captures the gains

questions.explanation: The text says snow "is increasingly unreliable" at lower altitudes, artificial snow "consumes water and energy", and survival depends "on a diversified economy".
questions.passage: Ski resorts in the Alps have been forced to confront the reality of warmer winters. At lower altitudes, snow is increasingly unreliable, and operators rely on artificial snow, which consumes water and energy. Some resorts have invested in summer attractions such as hiking, cycling and spas, hoping to become year-round destinations. Others have closed their lifts altogether. Critics of the artificial-snow strategy warn that it postpones adaptation rather than achieving it. The long-term survival of mountain communities, they argue, will depend on a diversified economy rather than on a season that is shortening.

items.q: What have warmer winters forced ski resorts to confront?

options: It is too expensive to make look real

questions.explanation: The text says "talent and the opportunity to develop it are unevenly distributed", it "can breed arrogance among winners and humiliation among losers", and a thoughtful position "acknowledges both points".
questions.passage: The notion of meritocracy, in which rewards go to those with talent and effort, has come under scrutiny. Critics note that talent and the opportunity to develop it are unevenly distributed, and that those who succeed are apt to attribute their success wholly to merit, forgetting luck and privilege. This can breed arrogance among winners and humiliation among losers. Defenders respond that a system based on merit is preferable to one based on birth. A thoughtful position acknowledges both points: that merit matters, and that a society should be cautious about assuming that those at the top are necessarily those who deserve it most.

items.q: What do critics note about talent and opportunity?
What can meritocracy breed?
options: Arrogance among winners and humiliation among losers

items.q: What does a thoughtful position acknowledge?
options: That merit matters but those at the top are not necessarily the most deserving

questions.explanation: The text says insects "pollinate crops, recycle nutrients and provide food", "data... are patchy", and the decline of small creatures "may prove more consequential".
questions.passage: A decline in the number of insects, the "insect apocalypse", has been reported in several countries, and its consequences may be far-reaching. Insects pollinate crops, recycle nutrients and provide food for birds and fish. Yet data on insect numbers are patchy, since few long-term surveys exist, and some scientists caution against sweeping conclusions. Even so, the available evidence from Europe and North America suggests that populations of many species have fallen. Probable causes include habitat loss, pesticides and warming. The decline of small creatures that most people ignore, researchers warn, may prove more consequential than that of the animals that attract attention.

items.q: What do insects do?
options: Pollinate crops, recycle nutrients and feed other animals

items.q: Why do some scientists caution?
What do researchers warn?
options: The decline of small creatures may be more consequential

questions.prompt: Read the text and answer the questions.
questions.explanation: The text says isolation "has preserved customs", a road means "young people leave for the cities, outside goods displace local crafts", and the thoughtful "stay with local families and buy what is made locally".
questions.passage: Remote villages in the mountains have long been accessible only by mule track, and their isolation has preserved customs that have vanished elsewhere. The arrival of a road, however welcome to residents who need a doctor or a market, tends to alter the pattern. Young people leave for the cities, outside goods displace local crafts and the village becomes a place of weekend houses. Travellers who value what they find there are therefore in a dilemma: their own visit contributes to the change they regret. The most thoughtful, villagers say, are those who arrive quietly, stay with local families and buy what is made locally.

items.q: What has preserved customs in mountain villages?
What often follows the arrival of a road?
options: Young people leave and outside goods displace crafts

items.q: Who are the most thoughtful visitors?
options: Those who arrive quietly, stay with locals and buy local goods
